title: Paleolithic Neanderthals Used Natural Aspirin
fact: Analysis of 50,000-year-old Neanderthal dental plaque revealed they self-medicated for pain using poplar bark, which contains the active ingredient in aspirin. They also ingested Penicillium mold, showing an awareness of natural antibiotics. Paleolithic hominids understood herbal medicine tens of thousands of years before modern science.

title: Stopping Cyclones With Hair Oil
fact: In 1896, famous scientist Jagadish Chandra Bose wrote the pioneering science fiction story নিরুদ্দেশের কাহিনী (Niruddesher Kahini, "Story of the Untraced"). In the tale, a character calms a massive cyclone by pouring a bottle of কুন্তলীন (Kuntaline, "hair oil") into the ocean. It surprisingly won a literary prize funded by the hair oil's creator.

title: The Empire That Stopped Alexander
fact: In 326 BCE, Alexander the Great halted his conquest of India because his weary troops feared the massive war-elephant army of গঙ্গাঋদ্ধি (Gangariddhi, "wealth of the Ganges"), an ancient empire centered in Bengal. Greek historians recorded that Bengal's ruler commanded thousands of battle-trained elephants, scaring the legendary army into turning back.

title: Speakers With An Internal Compass
fact: The Australian language Guugu Yimithirr completely lacks relative spatial terms like left or right. Instead, speakers use absolute cardinal directions for everything, saying things like there is an ant on your southwest leg. Consequently, native speakers possess a constant, flawless internal compass, even in pitch-black, unfamiliar caves.

title: Stone Age Chewing Gum DNA
fact: Mesolithic humans chewed birch bark pitch as ancient chewing gum, using it to relieve toothaches and glue tools. In 2019, scientists extracted a complete 5,700-year-old female human genome from a single chewed piece. The resin preserved her dark skin, blue eyes, oral bacteria, and a last meal of hazelnuts and mallard duck.

title: Noodles for the Goddess
fact: In Tangra, Kolkata, stands the চীনা কালীবাড়ি (Cheena Kalibari, "Chinese Kali Temple"), run by the local Chinese-Indian community. Uniquely, the priest offers stir-fried noodles and chop suey as প্রসাদ (proshad, "sacred food offering") to the Hindu deity instead of traditional sweets.

title: Feminist Sci-Fi in Ladyland
fact: In 1905, Bengali author Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain wrote Sultana's Dream, a futuristic tale where women rule using solar power while men are confined to the পুরুষখানা (purushkhana, "men's quarters"). Decades ahead of Western feminist sci-fi, she introduced flying cars and weather manipulation. Her amused husband called the story a delightful revenge.

title: The Lost Land Beneath the Sea
fact: Eight thousand years ago, Britain was connected to Europe by Doggerland, a thriving Mesolithic landscape of forests and lagoons. A massive underwater landslide later triggered a megatsunami that permanently submerged the region under the North Sea. Today, fishermen regularly dredge up Mesolithic bone harpoons and carved tools from the sea floor.

topic: History of language and how languages evolve
title: Ancient Roots of Everyday Words
fact: English and Hindi share a single ancestor language spoken 5,000 years ago called Proto-Indo-European. That is why basic everyday words like English mother and Bengali মা (ma, "mother") or English name and Hindi नाम (naam, "name") sound virtually identical. Linguists discovered this hidden global connection only in the late 18th century.

title: Nonsense Verse Born From Tragedy
fact: Sukumar Ray wrote his iconic collection of nonsense rhymes, আবোল তাবোল (Abol Tabol, "crazy tales"), while bedridden with an incurable fever. He corrected the final proofs from his deathbed, passing away just nine days before his masterpiece was published.

title: How Animal Spirits Created Steel
fact: Iron Age blacksmiths accidentally invented steel while trying to channel animal spirits into their weapons. They burned bones alongside iron ore, believing the animal's soul would inhabit the blade, which unwittingly introduced carbon into the iron. What they mistook for spiritual magic was actually the fundamental chemistry of steelmaking.

title: The Bankers Bigger Than England
fact: In 18th-century Bengal, the banking house of জগৎ শেঠ (Jagat Seth, "merchant of the world") in মুর্শিদাবাদ (Murshidabad, "city of Murshid") held wealth exceeding the Bank of England. They minted state currency and financed European trade networks before colonial takeover.
